strengths: The authors' core insight about efficient data usage in FL clients is valuable, as reducing unnecessary data sharing while maintaining performance is an important practical concern in real-world FL deployments.

Despite limitations, the paper provides extensive experiments across multiple standard datasets (CIFAR-10/100, FashionMNIST) and various FL aggregation methods (FedAvg, FedMedian, FedProx, etc.), demonstrating the framework's applicability across different settings.

This work provides an intuition that using all data from a client may not be the best option and develops a DRL algorithm to select the portion of data to use, which can achieve some empirical success.
Controlling the sampling rate is a known approach to cope with unbalanced data.
The idea of using RL to find the ratios is a nice idea.
Using reinforcement learning to optimize the amount of data per client in federated learning.
Provide some empirical and theoretical analysis of the proposed method.
weaknesses: The paper's core claim that "training a client locally on more data than necessary does not benefit overall performance" lacks rigorous theoretical justification; the provided proof in Section 4.4 shows only a trivial bound without connecting to the optimality of data selection.

In FL literature, there are many more advanced aggregation techniques addressing the imbalanced data problem (e.g., weighted aggregation); it is unclear how the proposed method works for different aggregation schemes.

Privacy preservation claims are made without formal analysis: no analysis or discussion of potential information leakage through the DRL agent's actions, and the implications of the agent observing client performance are missing.

The performance bound σ = π ω_c is a trivial result that merely states performance difference is bounded by area difference; no further analysis of convergence properties for the DRL training nor theoretical guarantees about the optimality of learned policies is provided.
The reward function design in eq. (8) seems arbitrary; the intuitions of this reward design choice are not explained.
The two proposed action selection strategies should be justified.
All figures show no statistical significance.
Only ResNet50 is used for experiments; it is unclear if the proposed method generalizes to different network architectures.
Comparison with other data selection strategies (such as [1] or simply weighted average) is missing.

The paper overlooks crucial related work in FL data selection and client optimization, including methods for client data pruning/selection, approaches using reinforcement learning for FL client selection (e.g., [1]), and recent work on personalized FL with data filtering.

Without comparison to related work, several claims about novelty need better contextualization: other works have explored adaptive data selection in FL, and the use of DRL for FL optimization is not new.
Fig.1(a) is hard to interpret without knowing the details later.
The term “optimal client” is misleading; it seems to mean optimized client instead.

L161 mentions that the algorithm can "guarantee that the data changes on the optimal client have little impact on the performance of other clients", which seems to be an empirical claim at best without any theoretical justification.

The ε‑greedy normalized cation in L198 is very questionable; normalization could be achieved by using a simple softmax for the policy network instead of using Eq.(3), and the summation in (4) should be the L1 norm for clarity.
Eq.(5) is not ε‑greedy; the ε case depends on the policy network, the max should be min instead, and the argmax computation for continuous actions is unclear.

L217 says the weighted metric action is "formally" given by (6), but this equation is not formally or mathematically accurate; the denominator should be the L1 norm of the difference, and it does not reflect L216’s condition of choosing only the classes with decreased performance.
In the first case of (7), the action may be out of bounds after adding the delta F1 scores, which is not handled explicitly in the paper.
Why do we need to switch after τ? (Questioning Eq.(8) motivation).
Why should the estimated loss use the form specified in L250?
Why is the same a_t used on both sides of the equation in L250 but they mean different things?
Why there is a ∇ in L258?
What are the REWARD_STEPS and EPISODE_LENGTH in L788 and 789?

L269's statement that "using more data leads to higher performance" directly contradicts the later claim that the performance of the Optimal Client will not be as good as if it was trained on its entire local dataset.
The results in L305‑339 are not related to the actual performance of the model for the clients; the so‑called performance in L315 does not have an interpretable meaning in the FL context.
Experiments have no comparison to other RL baselines; there is no comparison to other RL‑based selection/adjustment baselines (e.g., Wang et al., 2020, Nguyen et al., 2022).
The authors' work is very superficial: the state in RL is single dimensional, which clearly begs for more sophisticated state representations.
Section 3 first states that the state corresponds to the aggregated parameters, but then it is actually only the performance metric.
Using the term "Optimal Client" is very confusing and it is unclear what is the association with optimality.
When specifying actions, z_1, …, z_C are actually not used when imposing the lower and upper bounds.
The handling of the policy is unclear; it is a parametric policy but its form is never specified.
In DDPG the Q‑factor is used but advantage is more frequent.
The two theorems are very unclear; the proposition does not clearly state what is being claimed and seems to include only assumptions.
The theorem uses Ω which seems to be crucial but it is never defined; its definition appears only in the proof, which is too late.
The ablation study is actually not an ablation study; it is a robustness or sensitivity study with respect to data split.
There are many typos: \hat{f}_k and f_k are actually the same but the notation is different; in (8) T should be t, etc.

The term "optimal" in the title is misleading without any proof of optimality; such a strong claim should only be made when supported by provable theoretical optimality or extensive experimental analysis.
Figure 3 is directly taken from Richard Sutton’s Introduction to RL book without any modifications or credit, which constitutes plagiarism.
The main text is excessively long; the first five figures take up too much space and should be moved to the appendix or combined/reduced, and Algorithm 1 occupies excessive space unnecessarily.
The second paragraph of the introduction is overly long, discusses results in Figure 1 too early, and includes undefined concepts such as "normalized action" and "weighted metric action."
There are repetitive and inconsistent definitions of the term RL throughout the paper, and similarly inconsistent usage of "FL" versus "Federated Learning".
The experimental results are based on only one repetition, without any additional runs, making the results unreliable.
The experiments are conducted for only 8 clients; a more diverse and larger number of clients should be considered.
